subdivision.heading: Additional Rules Specific to Originating Applications for Judicial Review

operative_text.controlling:
3.15(1)  An originating application must be filed in the form of an
originating application for judicial review if the originating
applicant seeks from the Court any one or more of the following
remedies against a person or body whose decision, act or omission
is subject to judicial review:
(a) an order in the nature of mandamus, prohibition,
certiorari, quo warranto or habeas corpus;
(b) a declaration or injunction.
(2)  Subject to rule 3.16, an originating application for judicial
review to set aside a decision or act of a person or body must be
filed and served within 6 months after the date of the decision or
act, and rule 13.5 does not apply to this time period.
(3)  An originating application for judicial review must be served
on
(a) the person or body in respect of whose act or omission a
remedy is sought,
(b) the Minister of Justice or the Attorney General for
Canada, or both, as the circumstances require, and
(c) every person or body directly affected by the application.
(4)  The Court may require an originating application for judicial
review to be served on any person or body not otherwise required
to be served.
(5)  An affidavit or other evidence to be used to support the
originating application for judicial review, other than an originating
application for an order in the nature of habeas corpus, must be
filed and served on every other party one month or more before the
date scheduled for hearing the application.

Judicial review is a public law remedy only available against public bodies exercising public functions, and not against private organizations. One King's Bench judge cannot judicially review the decision of another, even if the decision was given as part of a statutory function.The doctrine ofpersona designatais gone in Alberta, and the remedy is an appeal.

An issue of private law, like contract, does not become a matter for judicial review just because a public body is involved. commentary.text: Rule 3.15 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.15. 1. Rule applies to municipal bylaws In Okotoks (Town) v. Foothills (Municipal District) No. 31, 2013 ABCA 222, the Court said, at paragraph 9: 9 … First, Okotoks submits that the enactment of a bylaw is not a “decision or act” of a body; hence Rule 3.15(2) does not apply. In our view, the Rule should not be read so narrowly. A municipal council can only act by resolution or bylaw: MGA section 180. Accordingly, we conclude that a bylaw is a decision or act of the municipality subject to the remedies in Rules 3.15(1)(a) and (b). In so holding, mindful of the nature of those remedies, we are not to be taken to have suggested that there exists some wide-ranging power to review the substance of bylaws for “reasonableness”. 2. Domestic tribunals In Falk v. Calgary Real Estate Board Co-Operative Ltd., 2000 ABQB 296, 2000 CarswellAlta 428, 265 A.R. 60, 82 Alta. L.R. (3d) 201, the plaintiff was “subject to the Board's tribunals by virtue of the voluntary contractual relationship between herself and the Board. Therefore, the Board's disciplinary tribunals are of a private or domestic nature” (p. 65). On the question of whether the judicial review provisions in the Rules of Court apply to consensual (domestic) tribunals, Rowbotham, J. said, at p. 66: I find that although the Board's disciplinary tribunals are domestic, their decisions are subject to judicial review for the limited purposes discussed in [Kaplan v. Canadian Institute of Actuaries (1994), 161 A.R. 321 (Q.B.); affirmed (1997), 206 A.R. 268 (C.A.); additional reasons at (1998), 212 A.R. 376, 168 W.A.C. 376, 60 Alta. L.R. (3d) 251 (C.A.); leave to appeal refused (1998), 227 N.R. 89 (note), 219 A.R. 160, 179 W.A.C. 160 (S.C.C.)]. The court is entitled to review the decisions to determine whether the tribunals have acted within their jurisdiciton; to ensure that decisions within their jurisdiction are not patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness. In Homestead Housing Co-operative Ltd. v. Barth, 2016 ABQB 538, 2016 CarswellAlta 1916 (Master), Master Schlosser said: 26 Can a private organization be judicially reviewed? Manderscheid J, in Slovenian Canadian (at para 29), after a review of authority, tells us that the Court can conduct a limited judicial review to determine whether (in that case) the Association violated its by-laws. In Lee v Yeung, Macklin J said (paras 29–31): 29 Despite the historical distinction between public and private law remedies, the courts have interpreted the Rules of Court as giving teeth to the declaratory remedy in the private law context. In Kaplan v Canadian Institute of Actuaries, 161 AR 321, [1994] A.J. No 868 (QB), Hunt J stated: 44 It seems to me that even if certiorari will not lie against a consensual tribunal, the court possesses broad enough powers under Rule 753.05 to grant the remedy it considers appropriate to the particular case, including the setting aside of an invalid decision or action … 30 In Falk v Calgary Real Estate Board Co-operative Ltd, 2000 ABQB 296, 265 AR 60, Rowbotham J considered Hunt J's reasoning in Kaplan and concluded: 13 I find that although the Board's disciplinary tribunals are domestic, their decisions are subject to judicial review for the limited purposes discussed in Kaplan, supra. The court is entitled to review the decisions to determine whether the tribunals have acted within their jurisdiction; to ensure that decisions within their jurisdiction are not patently unreasonable; and to prevent breaches of natural justice or fairness. In this case the decisions in question were within both tribunals' jurisdictions.
